01.note: When a relative of Rav Idi bar Avin died and left a date tree, another relative took it, each man insisting he was the closer relative. In the end the other man admitted that Rav Idi was closer, and Rav Hisda gave the tree to Rav Idi. Rav Idi then asked for the value of the dates the man had eaten since taking the tree. Rav Hisda scoffed at him: your claim rests on this man's word, and until now he said he was the closer relative, so the tree is yours only from his admission. The Gemara adds that Abaye and Rava disagree with Rav Hisda: once the man admitted, he admitted he never had a right to the fruit either.
01.why: The discussion is a run of disputes over who may keep land or its produce. The next case brought also ends with Abaye and Rava rejecting a ruling of Rav Hisda, so the two cases sit side by side.

people.name: Rav Idi bar Avin
people.about: Relative of the dead man who claims the date tree and the fruit already eaten from it

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: The judge who awards the tree to Rav Idi but refuses him the past produce

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Sage who, with Rava, disagrees with Rav Hisda's ruling on the produce

people.name: Rava
people.about: Sage who, with Abaye, disagrees with Rav Hisda's ruling on the produce

02.note: A man snatched a piece of cast metal from another. The victim came before Rabbi Ami, with Rabbi Abba sitting beside him, and brought a single witness to the snatching. The snatcher said: yes, I snatched it, but it was mine. Rabbi Ami was stuck: one witness is not enough to make him pay, but it is too much to let him go free, and he cannot be given an oath because by his own word he is like a robber. Rabbi Abba answered that someone who must take an oath but cannot take one has to pay.
02.why: Students before Abaye thought Rabbi Abba's case settled another one: a man claiming land who brought only one witness to his years of use. Abaye then shows the two cases are not alike, since there the single witness harms the man and here he helps him.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: The judge before whom the case of the snatched metal is brought

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: Sage sitting before Rabbi Ami who gives the ruling that settles the case

terms.meaning: In a money case, a defendant faced with only one witness against him can usually clear himself by swearing in court that the claim is false. The court does not let someone who admits to robbery swear.

03.note: Two men quarreled over a boat, each saying it was his. One asked the court to hold it until he could bring witnesses; Rav Huna said the court does so, Rav Yehuda said it does not. The court took the boat, but the man found no witnesses and asked the court to let it go so that whoever was stronger would win. Rav Yehuda said the court does not release it, and Rav Pappa said it does. The Gemara rules that a court does not seize such property, but once it has seized it, it does not let it go.
03.why: The discussion is about ownership disputes where neither side has proof. The next case applies the same rule, whoever is stronger prevails, and asks how it differs from cases where the property is split.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Sage who holds the court seizes the disputed boat

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Sage who holds the court neither seizes the boat nor, once seized, releases it

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Sage who holds the court releases the boat once no witnesses are found

terms.meaning: A ruling used when neither side has proof or a stronger claim: the court steps aside and lets the parties settle it between themselves.

04.note: In Neharde'a some goats ate a man's peeled barley. He seized the goats and claimed a large sum from their owner. Shmuel's father ruled he may claim up to the value of the goats, since he could have said the goats were his by purchase. The Gemara asks how that can be, when animals that wander do not show ownership just by being in someone's hands, and answers that goats are different because they are handed over to shepherds.
04.why: The Gemara has just discussed Reish Lakish's rule that holding wandering animals does not prove ownership, and Rava's rule for slaves. This case tests that rule with livestock, and the Gemara goes on to explain why Neharde'a goats are always under guard.

people.name: Shmuel's father
people.about: The judge who rules on the claim over the goats

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: Sage whose rule about wandering livestock the Gemara raises against the ruling

terms.meaning: The town in Babylonia where the case took place.
A standard claim: the one holding an item says he bought it. Holding it can back up that claim, so he may also make a smaller claim that is less than what that claim would give him.

05.note: Giddel bar Minyumi had a protest to lodge about his land. He found Rav Huna, Hiyya bar Rav and Rav Hilkiya bar Tuvi sitting together and protested before them. A year later he came back to protest again. They told him there was no need, because Rav says that once an owner has protested in the first year he need not protest again. Another version says Hiyya bar Rav told him this in his own name.
05.why: The Gemara is discussing how an owner protests against someone holding his land, so the holder cannot gain ownership by three years of use. Right after this case, bar Kappara's view and Rava's ruling say a protest is needed every three years.

people.name: Giddel bar Minyumi
people.about: Landowner who lodges a protest and comes back a year later to protest again

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: One of three Sages before whom he protests

people.name: Hiyya bar Rav
people.about: One of the three Sages; in one version he gives the answer himself

people.name: Rav Hilkiya bar Tuvi
people.about: One of the three Sages before whom he protests

people.name: Rav
people.about: Sage whose ruling the three cite: one protest in the first year is enough

terms.meaning: A formal objection by a landowner, made before witnesses, that someone is using his land wrongly. It stops the user from claiming ownership through three years of undisputed use.

06.note: A man went to betroth a woman, and she said she would marry him only if he signed all his property over to her. He did. His eldest son came and asked what would become of him. The father told two witnesses to hide in a place called Avar Yemina and write a gift document for the son. When the witnesses came before Rava, he ruled that neither the son nor the wife acquired the property.
06.why: Rav Yehuda has said a concealed gift document cannot be collected, and Rava was reported to hold that it cancels a later gift. Rav Pappa tells this case to show that report was only an inference; the Gemara then explains the wife lost because the gift to her was made under pressure.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The judge who rules that neither the son nor the wife acquired the property

terms.meaning: A gift document written in secret at the giver's request. Because it is hidden, the Sages suspect it was not meant seriously, and it cannot be used to collect.

07.note: A flood swept through Rav Anan's land and knocked down the boundary wall between his land and his neighbor's. Rav Anan rebuilt it but put it on his neighbor's land. Rav Nahman told him to move it back. Rav Anan objected that he had already taken possession, and Rav Nahman answered that the rule that possession in the owner's presence counts at once is not the law. Rav Anan said the neighbor had given up the land by helping him build the wall, and Rav Nahman replied that the neighbor did not know, just as Rav Anan did not.
07.why: The mishna has just taught that holding land proves nothing without a claim to it. This is the first of a series of cases, marked by a short memory aid, about when taking hold of land gives a right to it.

people.name: Rav Anan
people.about: Landowner who rebuilds his washed-out wall on his neighbor's land

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The judge who orders the wall moved back

terms.meaning: A right to land gained by using it openly, normally for three years, without the former owner protesting.

08.note: A flood swept through Rav Kahana's field and knocked down his boundary wall, and he rebuilt it on land that was not his. His neighbor brought two witnesses: one said the wall had gone two rows into the neighbor's land, the other said three. Rav Yehuda told Rav Kahana to pay two of the three rows. Rav Kahana asked if he was following Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who holds that witnesses who differ like this still combine for the smaller amount, and said he could bring a letter from the Land of Israel showing the law is not so. Rav Yehuda answered: when you bring it.
08.why: It follows Rav Anan's matching case of a wall rebuilt on a neighbor's land. Here the question shifts to two witnesses who do not agree on how much land was taken.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: Landowner who rebuilds his washed-out wall on land that is not his

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: The judge who orders Rav Kahana to pay two rows

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
people.about: Sage whose account of a dispute between the schools of Shammai and Hillel Rav Kahana cites

terms.meaning: The schools of the early Sages Shammai and Hillel, who often disagreed on points of law.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.
The Babylonian Sages' name for the Land of Israel.

09.note: A man had lived in a loft in Kashta for four years when the former owner came and asked what he was doing in his house. The man said he had bought it from someone who had bought it from the owner. Rabbi Hiyya told him that if he had witnesses that the seller had lived there, even for one day, the house would stay his; if not, it would not. Rav, his nephew, recalls asking him whether people do not often buy a house and sell it the same night, and he saw that Rabbi Hiyya would believe the man if he said the seller had bought it from the owner in his presence.
09.why: The discussion is about claims that come with holding land. Right after this, Rava tries to support Rabbi Hiyya's ruling from the mishna about inherited land, and the Gemara rejects the proof.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: The judge in the case of the loft; Rav calls him his uncle

people.name: Rav
people.about: Rabbi Hiyya's nephew, who sat before him and questioned his ruling

10.note: Abaye told Rava to come and see what the swindlers of Pumbedita do. A man asks a craftsman for his cloak back, and the craftsman says it never happened. The man says he has witnesses who saw it with him; the craftsman says that was a different cloak, and when asked to bring it out, he refuses. Rava answered that the craftsman's claim holds, since the owner must have seen his own cloak there. Rav Ashi said a clever owner can get him to bring it out by asking it to be valued against any debt, and Rav Aha son of Rav Avya replied that a clever craftsman can say it was already valued.
10.why: The Gemara has been teaching laws about items left with a craftsman, including a teaching that an owner has a claim only if he saw his item there. Rava uses that teaching to back the craftsman.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Sage who points out the trick of the Pumbedita craftsmen

people.name: Rava
people.about: Sage who holds that the craftsman's claim is accepted

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Sage who suggests how a clever owner can get the cloak brought out

people.name: Rav Aha, son of Rav Avya
people.about: Sage who answers Rav Ashi with the craftsman's counter-move

terms.meaning: A town in Babylonia known for its Torah academy.

10.flag: Not clearly a single event: Abaye describes a typical trick of Pumbedita craftsmen, and the rest is the Sages' back-and-forth about it.

11.note: A man named Tavi hung another man, Pafi, on a kinara and forced him to sell his field. Rabba bar bar Hana signed both Pafi's declaration that the sale was forced and the bill of sale. Rav Huna said that whoever signed the declaration did well, and whoever signed the bill of sale also did well.
11.why: The Gemara has just ruled that a sale made under force is valid. It then asks how Rav Huna can approve both documents, and explains him by his own rule that a forced sale stands.

people.name: Tavi
people.about: Man who hangs Pafi and forces him to sell his field

people.name: Pafi
people.about: Man forced to sell his field

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: Sage who signs both the declaration and the bill of sale

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Sage who says both signings were right

terms.meaning: Usually understood as a kind of tree or thorn bush; Pafi was hung on one to force him to sell.
A statement made before witnesses ahead of a sale or gift, saying it is being done under force and is not truly wanted. It can cancel the transaction.
The document that records a sale of land.

12.note: When the wife of Rabba bar bar Hana was dying, she said that rings she had belonged to Marta and to the sons of her daughter. Rabba bar bar Hana came before Rav to ask what to do. Rav told him: if she is credible in your eyes, do as she said; if not, ignore her words. Another version says Rav told him to judge how likely it was that the rings had been left with her.
12.why: A teaching the Gemara has just quoted says that when a woman, slave or child declares at death that an item belongs to someone, the bailee follows them if believable and ignores them if not. Rav applies that rule to this case.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: Husband who asks what to do with the rings after his wife's dying words

people.name: Rav
people.about: Sage who tells him how to treat her words

people.name: Marta
people.about: Person his wife named as owner of the rings

13.note: A woman had cut branches from an ownerless palm tree for thirteen years. Then another man came and plowed a little beneath it. The case came before Levi, or by another account Mar Ukva, who gave the tree to the man who plowed. The woman came and shouted before him, and he said to her: what can I do for you, since you did not take possession the way people take possession?
13.why: Shmuel has been listing acts that do or do not acquire ownerless land, depending on whether they improve the field. This case shows that years of cutting branches did not count, while a little plowing did.

people.name: Levi
people.about: Sage before whom the case came in one version

people.name: Mar Ukva
people.about: Sage before whom the case came in another version, who answers the woman

terms.meaning: Land or goods that belong to no one, such as the estate of a convert who died without heirs. The first person to perform a proper act of possession acquires it.

14.note: Rav Huna bought land from a non-Jew, and another Jew came and plowed it a little. They came before Rav Nahman, who gave the land to the man who plowed. Rav Huna asked whether he was relying on Shmuel's rule that a non-Jew's property is like a desert, open to the first who takes it. If so, he said, let him also follow Shmuel's other rule, that one who hoes acquires only the spot he hoed. Rav Nahman answered that on this point he follows the teaching that one stroke of the hoe acquires the whole field.
14.why: The Gemara has quoted Shmuel's rule about land bought from a non-Jew, and Abaye has questioned it because land law requires a deed. This case shows the rule being applied, and a ruling follows that the land is not taken from the second Jew.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Buyer of land from a non-Jew, which another Jew then plowed

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The judge who gives the land to the man who plowed

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Sage whose two rulings Rav Huna quotes

people.name: Rav
people.about: Sage whose ruling that one stroke of a hoe acquires the whole field Rav Nahman follows

terms.meaning: Ownerless. Shmuel's term for land a non-Jew has sold for money but whose buyer has not yet received the deed.

15.note: Rabbi Bena'a was marking burial caves. At the cave of Abraham he found Eliezer, Abraham's servant, standing at the entrance, who told him Abraham was lying in Sarah's arms while she examined his head. Rabbi Bena'a asked to be announced; Eliezer told him to enter, since in that world there is no evil inclination, and he went in, examined the cave and left. At Adam's cave a Divine Voice told him he had looked at the likeness of God's image but must not look at the image itself, and that the inner cave measures the same as the outer. Rabbi Bena'a says he saw Adam's heels, and they were like two suns.
15.why: The Gemara has been quoting teachings about how Torah scholars keep their tables and beds. It says it tells this story because Rabbi Bena'a was just mentioned.

people.name: Rabbi Bena'a
people.about: Sage marking burial caves who enters the cave of Abraham

people.name: Eliezer
people.about: Abraham's servant, standing at the cave entrance

people.name: Abraham
people.about: Lies in the cave in Sarah's arms

people.name: Sarah
people.about: Abraham's wife, examining his head

people.name: Adam
people.about: The first man, whose cave Rabbi Bena'a is told not to look into; he saw his heels

terms.meaning: Graves were marked so that priests and others could avoid becoming ritually impure by contact with the dead.
A voice from heaven that speaks in Talmud stories.
The urge in a person toward sin, here including sexual desire.

16.note: A magus was rummaging through graves. When he reached the burial cave of Rav Tovi bar Mattana, Rav Tovi grabbed him by the beard and would not let go. Abaye came and begged him to release the man. A year later the magus came again, and Rav Tovi grabbed his beard again. This time he would not let go even when Abaye asked, until Abaye brought scissors and cut off the beard.
16.why: It follows the story of Rabbi Bena'a marking burial caves, as another tale about burial caves.

people.name: Rav Tovi bar Mattana
people.about: Dead Sage in whose burial cave the magus is caught

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Sage who asks Rav Tovi to release the magus, and in the end cuts off the beard

terms.meaning: A Persian priest. The Gemara often mentions them disturbing graves.

17.note: A dying man told his family: a barrel of earth to one son, a barrel of bones to another, and a barrel of wads of wool to a third. No one knew what he meant, so they came to Rabbi Bena'a. He asked whether their father had left land, livestock and quilts, and they said yes. Then that was his meaning, he told them: land to one son, livestock to the second and quilts to the third.
17.why: It is the first of a set of Rabbi Bena'a stories, told after the account of him marking burial caves.

people.name: Rabbi Bena'a
people.about: Sage who works out the dying man's riddle

18.note: A man overheard his wife tell their daughter to keep her affairs hidden, since she herself had ten sons and only one was by the girl's father. When he was dying he said: all my property to one son. The family did not know which, and came to Rabbi Bena'a. He told the sons to go strike their father's grave until he rose and told them; they all went except one, and Rabbi Bena'a gave everything to the one who stayed away. The other brothers, angry, slandered him at the king's court as a man who takes people's money without witnesses, and he was arrested and imprisoned. The text here does not say how it ended.
18.why: It is one of a series of stories about Rabbi Bena'a's wisdom, told after the account of him marking burial caves.

people.name: Rabbi Bena'a
people.about: Sage who finds out which son is the dying man's true son, and is imprisoned for it

18.flag: The story stops at Rabbi Bena'a's imprisonment; how he got out (his wife's riddle) follows straight on and may belong to the same story.

19.note: While Rabbi Bena'a was in prison, his wife told the guards a riddle: she had one servant whose head they cut off, whom they skinned and ate, filled with water and gave friends to drink from, without paying her. No one understood, so they called the wise man of the Jews, Rabbi Bena'a, who explained that she meant a goat made into a water skin. Impressed, they had him sit as a judge at the gate. He corrected two inscriptions there: a judge summoned to court is unfit only if money is lawfully taken from him, and blood is first of all illness, wine first of all healing. Each time they added: the elders of the Jews say so.
19.why: It continues the Rabbi Bena'a stories: after his ruling about the dead man's sons, his brothers had him put in prison, and this is how he got out.

people.name: Rabbi Bena'a
people.about: Imprisoned Sage who explains his wife's riddle and becomes a judge at the gate

people.name: The wife of Rabbi Bena'a
people.about: Tells the guards a riddle while her husband is in prison

terms.meaning: The city gate, where judges sat to hear cases.

19.flag: Starts in the middle: the reason Rabbi Bena'a is in prison is told just before, in the preceding story.

20.note: Rabbi Ami had a projection from his house sticking out into an alleyway. Another man had one sticking out into the public street, and the public objected. He came before Rabbi Ami, who told him to cut it off. The man said: but you have one too. Rabbi Ami answered that his own stuck out into an alleyway, whose few residents had agreed to it, while the man's stuck out into the public street, and no one can agree on behalf of the public.
20.why: The mishna has just taught that one may not build projections or balconies out over the public domain. Rabbi Ami's case applies that rule and is followed by a similar story about Rabbi Yannai and a tree.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Sage with a projection into an alleyway who orders the man to cut his own

terms.meaning: A beam or part of a building that sticks out from the wall over the street or alley.
Streets and places that belong to everyone, not to particular residents.
